title: Miscarriage care
what: Care when a pregnancy has stopped developing or a miscarriage has begun. The doctor checks whether everything has passed from the womb and helps finish the process gently.
why: For bleeding and pain in early pregnancy, or when an ultrasound shows the pregnancy has stopped developing.
duration: the exam and ultrasound take about an hour; treatment takes from a few hours to 1 to 2 weeks, depending on the method
tell_doctor: When the bleeding and pain started
Your blood type and Rh factor

prepare.title: Options
prepare.text: Your doctor will explain the options: wait, take pills, or have a short procedure. Together you will decide what suits you.

prepare.title: Food
prepare.text: If you have a procedure under anesthesia, usually no food for 6 hours. Check with your doctor.

prepare.title: Someone close
prepare.text: Ask someone close to be with you and take you home.

steps: The doctor examines you and does an ultrasound
The doctor explains what has happened and what the options are
If you wait, you go home with a plan and a number to call
If pills, you take them, and tissue passes within a few hours
If a procedure, under brief anesthesia the doctor gently empties the womb through the cervix, with no cuts
After 1 to 2 weeks, a follow-up exam or ultrasound
feel: Pain like a heavy period, and bleeding
Grief, guilt, and confusion are natural. Do not hesitate to ask for support
after: Bleeding usually lasts up to 2 weeks
No tampons, swimming, or sex until the bleeding stops
If you are Rh negative, you may need an anti-D injection
Talk to your doctor about a new pregnancy. They will say when it is OK
Most often, a miscarriage is chance, not your fault
red_flags: Soaking 2 large pads an hour for 2 hours in a row: call emergency services
Severe belly pain or fainting: call emergency services
A fever over 38°C (100.4°F), or bad-smelling discharge: see a doctor urgently

faq.a: Almost always not. Most often a miscarriage happens because of a random chromosome error.
Usually after your first period, if you feel ready. Check with your doctor.
Often yes: by waiting or taking pills. Your doctor will say what is safe for you.

reminders.text: Doctor's visit tomorrow. Bring pads and your ultrasound results. Ask someone close to be with you.
